title: The thirty-three swayyas
hook: verses on true devotion and against empty ritual

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chandi di Var: a war ballad whose first stanza opens the Ardas. Your line was the power remembered. What did you pause before? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-eight.

A uniform tells you what someone is supposed to be. It doesn't tell you what they are. A white coat, a badge, a robe, a turban, a cross on a chain: each one makes a promise on the outside. Traditions have had to ask what happens when the outside and the inside don't match. Guru Gobind Singh asks it in a set of verses in a form called the swayya. There are thirty-three of them, and they keep circling one question: what does real devotion look like, under the clothes?
screen: `A UNIFORM MAKES A PROMISE.` → `OUTSIDE AND INSIDE.` → `THIRTY-THREE SWAYYAS.`

segments.voice: A swayya is a verse form, a stanza with a strong, rolling beat, good for reciting aloud. The thirty-three swayyas sit among Guru Gobind Singh's writings, and the first one says who is Khalsa. Paraphrased: the one who remembers, day and night, the light that never goes out; who brings no one but the One into the mind; who is full of love and trust; who does not, even by mistake, put faith in fasts, tombs, shrines and outward rites; who knows the One beyond pilgrimage, charity, austerity and self-control. When that perfect light shines in the heart, know that one as Khalsa, pure. Look at the order. The light comes first. The love and trust come next. The outward things are not mocked for fun; they're simply moved out of the center. Pilgrimage and charity aren't called evil. They're called not enough, on their own, without the One. Other swayyas in the set are sharper. They turn on people who wear religious dress to impress, or to collect money from the faithful, while their hearts are elsewhere. That edge isn't aimed at one community. It's aimed at a habit any community can fall into, Sikhs included, and some Sikh teachers read it that way: as a mirror for their own house first. So the verses ask a hard, simple thing. Not, what do you wear, or where have you traveled, but is the light awake inside?
screen: `A SWAYYA: A ROLLING VERSE.` · `THE LIGHT THAT NEVER GOES OUT.` · `NOT EVIL, JUST NOT ENOUGH.` · `A MIRROR FOR YOUR OWN HOUSE.` · then, large: `TRUE DEVOTION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one swayya. If you can find the first of the thirty-three, read it slowly, once, in any language. If you can't, take the paraphrase you just heard. Then sit with one question, gently: which of my habits are outside, and which are inside? Don't judge either list. Just notice. Then let the question go, and rest your attention on the breath, as if it were a small light that doesn't go out. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on the breath. The bell holds the time.
The thirty-three swayyas. Verses by Guru Gobind Singh on true devotion; the first says the Khalsa is the one in whom the perfect light shines. Today's word.
Your line: true devotion. Today, do one good thing in a way nobody will see or thank you for, and let that be the whole point. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite the first of Guru Gobind Singh's thirty-three swayyas when teaching what it means to be Khalsa, and the set is read in katha as a call to inner devotion over outward show.

original.note: Gurmukhi: Khalsa. the first swayya says who deserves the name: the one in whom the perfect light shines.

trapdoor: what you thought: old verses against other people's rituals.
what it means: verses asking what devotion looks like under the clothes. outward forms are not enough on their own.
what a scholar hears: the first swayya defines Khalsa by an inner light, and Sikh teachers read the sharper verses as a mirror for their own house.
